In Opposition to

LD 652, An Act to Provide Qualifying Downtown Businesses and

Developments with Assistance Paying Flood Insurance Premiums

March 5, 2025

Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Taxation, my name is Amanda Campbell, and I am submitting testimony in opposition to LD 652 on
behalf of the Maine Municipal Association's 70-member Legislative Policy Committee (LPC).

LD 652 would expand the eligible costs related to Tax Increment Financing (TIF) District revenue to
includeestablishing and funding a flood assistance program to assist businesses and developments with
flood insurance. This new eligible cost would be limited to a value not to exceed 25% of the TIF district's
captured value.

As the Department of Economic and Community Development (DECD) has stated in prior testimony, TIF revenues must be used to further the economic development interests of the community. The proposed

usage of funds to assist businesses with an operating expense directly related to a deliberate decision to

maintain an establishment in the flood zone certainly strays from the original investment intentions of TIF

law. TIF revenues to assist businesses would be better spent on relocating those businesses to a

sustainable location out of harms way. In these times of resilience and hazard mitigation, incentivizing

business and development in potentially hazardous areas is counterproductive and puts bad money before

good.

'

'

Thank you for your consideration of the municipal perspective on this important topic. Please feel free to
contact any member of the LPC or the MMA Advocacy team with any questions relating to municipal
operations.

TESTIMONY ON LD 652 BEFORE THE TAXATION COMMITTEE
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and Honorable Members of the Taxation
Committee. I am Representative David Rollins, and I have come before you to present LD 652,
An Act to Provide Qualifying Downtown Businesses and Developments with Assistance Paying
Flood Insurance.
According to the Maine Emergency Management Agency flooding can happen anytime,
anywhere, and not necessarily near the coast, lakes, or rivers. In recent years, about 25% of
national flood insurance claims came from places not considered high risk for flooding. Flooding can be caused by hurricanes, tropical storms, heavy rain, ice jams, fast melting snow and dam failures. Just a few inches of water can cause thousands of dollars' worth of damage to a home
or business.
The National Flood insurance Program (NFIP) was created by Congress in response to the rising cost of disaster relief for flood victims. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) manages it.
Maine's average cost of flood insurance per county. York County has the cheapest rates at $977 per year, while rates in Kennebec County are the most expensive at $1,787 per year... this is according to Money Geek. According to an Al overview, "ln 2020, Maine's flood damage was $191 million and is expected to increase to $25 million by 2050. Flooding is a threat yearround in Maine but is most likely to occur in the spring."
Flood insurance is not mandatory in Maine at the state level. However, it may be required by
mortgage lenders, especially for properties in high-risk flood zones.
The purpose of this bill is to assist businesses and development in qualified downtown districts with help in procuring flood insurance to help lessen the economic impact to the business, city or town and state. Further, to assist economic development in the affected areas of downtown
districts across all of Maine.
Attached is a list of eligible costs under the Maine TIF Statute. l encourage you to add flood insurance as an eligible cost to create and presen/e economic development in downtown districts throughout Maine. l submit this bill and ask for a unanimous vote of "Ought to Pass."

Testimony of Keith Luke
Economic Development Director, City of Augusta In Support of LD 652 - An Act to Provide Qualifying Downtown Businesses and Developments with Assistance Paying Flood Insurance Premiums Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation March 2025
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation, my name is Keith Luke, and I serve as
the Economic Development Director for the City of Augusta. I am here today
to testify in strong support of LD 652, An Act to Provide Qualifying Downtown
Businesses and Developments with Assistance Paying Flood Insurance Premiums.
The concept for this legislation first took shape following the devastating floods that struck Central Maine in 2024 and again in early 2025. I began work on this proposal with our former State Representative, Raegan LaRochelle,
who shared my concern about the long-term economic consequences of
these events for Maine's historic downtowns.
LD 652 seeks to create a valuable tool for municipalities to support reinvestment in their downtowns by allowing Tax Increment Financing (TI F) revenues to fund locally managed programs that would reimburse property owners for a portion of their flood insurance premiums. These programs would be fully designed and administered at the local level, ensuring that they are tailored to meet each community's unique needs.
This bill serves a two-fold purpose. First, it encourages existing building owners to enroll in flood insurance coverage, providing an essential safety net in the event of future flooding. Second, it helps to reduce a well-documented financial barrier that discourages potential investors from acquiring and
redeveloping downtown properties.
As you know, conventional lenders routinely require flood insurance before issuing mortgages for buildings located within flood hazard zones. Yet, the
rising cost of this insurance -- particularly through the National Flood Insurance Program --- often makes downtown redevelopment projects

financially unworkable. This legislation provides municipalities with a powerfultoolto help close that gap.
lt's important to acknowledge that, while some may question the wisdom of investing in flood-prone areas, the reality is that Maine's downtowns -- including those in Augusta, Gardiner, Saco, Hallowell, and Bangor- have
always been and will continue to be centered on our rivers and waterfronts.
People want to live, work, and invest near the water, and we as communities
actively encourage this through our economic development strategies.
LD 652 helps ensure that these critical historic and economic assets can continue to thrive, contributing to the vitality and resiliency of Maine's
downtowns. By providing financial assistance for flood insurance, we can
lower the barriers to investment and ensure that our downtowns remain places where businesses want to locate, where entrepreneurs want to invest and where our communities can grow stronger-- even in the face of a
changing climate.
I urge you to support LD 652, and i welcome any questions you may have.
Thank you.

TESTIMONY OF MICHAEL J. ALLEN, ASSOCIATE COMMISSIONER FOR TAX POLICY
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND FINANCIAL SERVICES
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation Hearing Date: March 5, 2025
LD 652 - "An Act to Provide Qualifying Downtown Businesses and Developments with Assistance Paying Flood Insurance Premiums"
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and members of the Taxation Committee - good morning, my name is Michael Allen, Associate Commissioner for Tax Policy in the Department of Administrative and Financial Services. I am testifying at the request of the Administration Neither For Nor Against LD 652, "An Act to Provide Qualifying Downtown Businesses and Developments with Assistance Paying Flood Insurance Premiums."
I am submitting this testimony to raise two technical concerns with the bill's language. First, the bill summary states that the new described costs are allowed for municipalities/plantations with established downtown tax increment financing districts, but the bill language does not appear to limit it to only downtown districts. This should be clarified.
Second, the bill does not include these new project costs in 30-A M.R.S. � 5249, which details allowable project costs for affordable housing development districts. It is unclear whether the bill intends to exclude these costs from the affordable housing districts or whether this was an oversight. This should also be clarified.
Any administrative costs associated with the bill can be absorbed under current budgetary allotments.
